It is helpful to estimate the relative potencies of G and v on the scale of the microstructure to be expected, for example the primary dendrite arm spacing, Lp.

In order to do this, consider first the temperature interval, AT₁, required for solidifi- cation to be completed. If the phase diagram is taken to be a binary one with a liquidus of slope m and a solid/liquid partitioning coefficient of k, then it can be demonstrated that To is given by mco(k – 1)/k, where co is the bulk composition of the alloy under consideration. The scale of the dendritic structure is then as depicted in Figure 3.26. The dendrites are assumed to possess a radius of curvature R at their tips, which are spaced a distance Lp apart. The mean height of the dendrite trunks is then ∆To/G, where G is the temperature gradient; the thickness of the trunks at their roots is given the symbol λ, which is approximately one half of Lp. A steady-state is assumed – thus, the dendritic structure translates at a velocity v, and its shape is invariant as it does so. A first esti- mate of the radius of curvature of the tip of each dendrite is given by fitting a parabola to its shape [22]; from elementary geometry, it is then equal to the ratio of the square of the minor axis of the parabola (which is equal to λ) to the major axis (∆Το/G) – so that R = λ2G/ΔΤο.

For the solidification conditions pertinent to the superalloys, there are two contributions to the total undercooling AT. The first is due to the solutal undercooling, ∆Tsolutal, arising from the partitioning of solute; the second, ATcurvature, is a consequence of the Gibbs–Thomson

Consistent with the growth of an isolated dendrite tip, see the Appendix to this chapter, the super- saturation, Ω, is given by Ω = Rv/D, where D is the diffusion coefficient of solute in the liquid ahead of the front. Making this substitution, along with R = λ2G/∆To, one has

Equation (3.14) represents an expression for the dependence of the undercooling, AT, upon the three variables λ = Lp/2, G and v. One of these can be eliminated using a further equation or criterion [22]. For example, one can invoke the extremum condi- tion, which states that growth will occur at whatever a minimises ΔT or maximises v. This implies that ∆T/8λ = 0; after some algebraic manipulation, one can show that

3.2 Optimisation of the chemistry of single-crystal superalloys

Over a period of about 20 years, the chemistry of the single-crystal superalloys has been refined in order to improve the properties displayed. Although much of this progress has been incremental, a clear picture has emerged of the roles played by the various elements in conferring the best properties. Whilst it should be remembered that the various alloy producers and engine manufacturers have settled on proprietary chemistries to maintain their competitive advantage, the compositions of the single-crystal superalloys have evolved significantly in the period since 1980 when the first ones emerged. The compositions of important first-, second-, third- and fourth-generation single-crystal superalloys are given in Tables 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5. Of note is the introduction of significant additions of Re, and the reduction of Ti and Mo to low concentrations. Some interesting insights into the early alloy development efforts are given in refs. [24] and [25]. With the benefit of hindsight, the improvements in performance have been won by respecting the four guidelines set out on pp. 152-170.

content_blocks.content: 3.2.1 Guideline 1
Proportions of y'-forming elements such as Al, Ti and Ta should be high, such that the γ' fraction is ~70%.

Why is 70% an appropriate figure? To answer this question, one must have an apprecia- tion of the micromechanisms of creep deformation in the single-crystal superalloys. This is discussed in more detail in Section 3.3, but here it is sufficient to note that, across a wide range of temperature and levels of applied stress, creep deformation on the microscale is restricted to the y channels which lie between the precipitates of γ'. Thus, creep dis- locations do not penetrate the y' precipitates. It follows then that a reduced fraction of y yields improved properties. The optimum microstructure then consists of many fine y' particles with very thin layers of the y matrix separating them; see Figure 3.28. This can be rationalised by making a rough estimate of the Orowan stress, Tloop, following ref. [26]. This is approximately Gb/l, where G is the shear modulus, b is the Burgers vector and I is the width of the y' channel. With G = 50 GPa, b = 0.25 nm and 1 = 100 nm, this yields 125 MPa. For uniaxial loading along (100), the Schmid factor assuming {111}(110) slip is 1/√6; the applied stress for bowing is then 306 MPa. This is significant, and is one of the major reasons why the single-crystal superalloys perform so well at elevated temperatures.

A second point is that the creep performance does not increase monotonically as the y' fraction is increased – thus, an alloy with 70% γ' performs better than one with 100% γ'. This implies a strong strengthening effect from the y/y' interfaces, which impart resistance to creep deformation. This effect has been confirmed by measuring the creep rupture lives of a series of alloys containing various fractions of y' of identical composition [27]. The set of tie-lines characterising a multicomponent alloy of interest was first determined, and a family of related alloys cast with chemistries chosen such that the compositions of both y and y' were identical in all cases. With respect to the optimisation of the chemistry, it is useful to consider the Ni-Al binary diagram. At 700 °C, the solubility of Al in Ni is about 10 at%. The Ni3Al has an Al content of 25 at%. Therefore, in the binary system one needs a composition, ē, satisfying (ē – 10)/(25 – 10) = 0.75. Hence ē = 21.25 at%. This corresponds to about 11 wt%. A modern single-crystal superalloy would have about 6 wt% Al. Clearly, significant reliance is being placed on the y'-forming elements such as Ta and Ti.

Thus the balance of y - and y'-forming elements must be chosen such that the y' fraction is optimal. But there is another consideration. There should exist a sufficient solutioning window, AT, below the melting temperature, across which y is the only stable phase. This is necessary because, after solidification, heat treatment is required to remove residual microsegregation and eutectic mixtures rich in γ'. This puts the y' precipitates into solution; during subsequent exposure to lower temperatures, the y' develops a uniform microstructure with an optimum precipitate size. The heat treatment for a typical single-crystal superalloy such as CMSX-4 would involve a solutioning of 8h at 1314°C, a primary age of 4h at 1140°C followed by a secondary age of 16h at 870°C. Figure 3.30 shows a prediction of the phase stability of the CMSX-4 superalloy around the melting temperature. The solutioning window is about 50°C, which is rather small; this emphasises the need for precise temperature control during heat treatment. 3.2.2 Guideline 2
The composition of the alloy must be chosen such that the y /γ' lattice misfit is small; this minimises the y/y' interfacial energy so that y' coarsening is restricted.

The lattice misfit, δ, is defined according to
δ = 2 x (αγ' - αγ) / (αγ' + αγ) (3.17)
where the lattice parameters of the y and y' phases, ay and ayı, respectively, depend via Vegard's law on the elemental compositions in each phase, and consequently on the extent of γ/γ' partitioning. For the y phase, one has, to a good approximation (refer to Figure 2.18),
αγ = 3.524 + 0.110xCr + 0.478xMo +0.444xw + 0.441xRe +0.179xAl +0.422xTi + 0.700xTa (3.18)
where the xiγ are the mole fractions of i in y, and the various constants are taken from correlations such as those given in Chapter 2. For the y' phase, one finds
Αγ' = 3.570 – 0.004xCr + 0.208xMo + 0.194xw + 0.262xRe + 0.258xTi + 0.500xTa (3.18b)

where the mole fractions are now evaluated in that phase. The value of the misfit has been found to exhibit a significant effect on the morphology of the y' precipitates [28]; see Figure 3.31. When the misfit is small, less than about 0.5%, the y' particles are cuboids
